title: Buckner Site — Fort Ancient villages on Strodes Creek
summary: In Bourbon County, the Buckner Site holds two circular Fort Ancient villages around plazas, occupied mainly from about A.D. 1200 to 1400.
bodyMarkdown:
The Buckner site is an archaeological site in Bourbon County, in the heart of the Inner Bluegrass. It belongs to the Middle Fort Ancient period, which [Wikipedia dates to about 1200–1400 CE](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckner_Site_%2815BB12%29). Its builders were Native farming families who lived in Kentucky centuries before any European arrived.

## Two villages around two plazas

According to [an account of the Buckner Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buckner_Site_%2815BB12%29), Buckner has two large circular village areas. Each one surrounds its own central plaza. Several smaller special-use areas lie to the north and northeast of the main villages.

That plan fits a wider Fort Ancient pattern. [Grokipedia's Fort Ancient article](https://grokipedia.com/page/Fort_Ancient) describes villages laid out in circles or rectangles around a central plaza used for ceremonies and gatherings. Houses were built of wattle and daub on wooden posts, set in shallow basins or wall trenches.

## The Fort Ancient world

The Fort Ancient people farmed maize and lived in villages along the middle Ohio Valley. Grokipedia says they made shell-tempered cordmarked pottery, triangular projectile points and bone tools. Their villages were often enclosed by palisades.

Grokipedia calls the Middle Phase, about 1250 to 1450 CE, a time of peak growth. Population rose, and settlements became larger and more complex. Many villages were stockaded with wooden posts, which suggests defensive needs as communities grew. Grokipedia also notes that circular village plans with plazas and burial areas point to rule by elders or councils rather than hereditary chiefs.

The Late Phase, from about 1450 to 1750 CE, brought climate stress and more conflict, and Fort Ancient communities eventually dispersed. Kentucky sites from that later era include [Hardin Village](/stories/hardin-village-15gp22/) and [Fox Farm](/stories/fox-farm-mason-county/).

## Excavation in the Depression

Buckner was excavated in the 1930s by William S. Webb, according to Wikipedia. The work was salvage archaeology carried out during the Great Depression. Webb, a University of Kentucky physics professor, became the first head of the university's new department of archaeology and anthropology in 1926, [a biography of Webb](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_S._Webb) says. Beginning in 1933, he also coordinated excavations in the Tennessee Valley.

Depression-era projects like these recorded many Kentucky sites before farming or construction could damage them. Other Fort Ancient villages in the Bluegrass include [Singer-Hieronymus](/stories/singer-hieronymus-fort-ancient-villages-on-north-elkhorn/) and the [Muir site](/stories/muir-site-early-fort-ancient-on-a-jessamine-ridge/).

## National Register listing

The site was added to the National Register of Historic Places on January 27, 1983. The [National Park Service's NPGallery record](https://npgallery.nps.gov/AssetDetail/NRIS/83002557) lists its significance as prehistoric, with a period of significance of 1000–1499 AD. The record keeps the site's address restricted, which is standard protection for archaeological sites.

## Kentucky today

Buckner is an archaeological site, and this story gives its county only. Bourbon County later drew settlers such as [Capt. John Strode](/stories/capt-john-strode-of-strodes-station/), but its farmland was home to Native villages long before that. The site deserves respect as a place where Native families lived and farmed.
